ut.title: Ultrasonic Testing & Thickness Testing | Tacoma, WA
ut.description: Ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection in Tacoma, WA for cranes, tideflats piping, tanks, vessels and bridge steel. Technicians mobilize. Quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Tacoma, Washington
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT carries out ultrasonic thickness testing and ultrasonic weld inspection in Tacoma, Washington, for waterfront cranes, process piping and tanks on the tideflats, vessels, bridge steel and heavy fabrications around Commencement Bay. Technicians are mobilized to your terminal, plant or yard with calibrated instruments and a written procedure, and readings are reported against the code or specification you name. To start a scope, use the Tacoma UT inspection quote request; we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is needed in Tacoma

Tacoma is a working harbor. The port is a naturally deepwater harbor on Commencement Bay in south Puget Sound, with container terminals operated through the Northwest Seaport Alliance and roughly 2,500 acres of port-owned land hosting a mix of maritime and industrial tenants. Ship-to-shore container cranes, rail-mounted gantries and heavy-lift equipment are all welded steel structures that live in salt air and see cyclic loading every working day. Their boom girders, backreach frames, legs and sill beams are classic places for ultrasonic weld examination and for thickness checks on corroded members. Along the waterways behind the terminals, the tideflats hold fuel and chemical storage, a pulp and paperboard industry, metals processing and an LNG facility, each with tanks, vessels and process piping whose walls thin with time.

Away from the water, Tacoma's history in smelting and shipbuilding left a base of fabricators and repair yards, and the Tacoma Narrows crossings and other steel bridges of the Puget Sound region keep state transportation crews busy. Pipe racks, pressure vessels at pulp and paper operations, and water and wastewater plants complete the picture. For almost all of it, the wall thickness of a pipe or vessel is a number that someone needs, and ultrasonic testing provides it without taking the system apart.

What ultrasonic testing can and cannot tell you

An ultrasonic instrument sends a short sound pulse through a probe into the steel and measures the time taken for the echo to return. On a plain plate that time gives thickness; on a weld, the pattern of echoes from within the metal marks the location and approximate size of a flaw. The strength of UT is that it looks through the metal, so it can find internal corrosion on a pipe wall and planar defects deep in a weld that no surface method would see. Its weaknesses are practical. The surface must be clean and smooth enough for the probe to couple, and thick marine paint, scale or barnacle residue gets in the way. Wet, corroded and pitted surfaces scatter sound. Austenitic and cast welds with coarse grains blur the signal. And UT gives information at the points scanned, so the survey plan has to put the readings where the damage is likely to be.

Thickness surveys on piping, tanks and cranes

Thickness work follows the contact pulse-echo method in ASTM E797 and ASME Section V Article 5, with SE-797 in Article 23. Corroded surfaces call for dual-element probes, which keep transmitter and receiver apart and cope better with rough metal. The instrument is calibrated on a step block made from material of matching sound velocity, and the technician checks the A-scan trace to be sure the echo is the true back wall and not a lamination or a doubled signal on a thin point. Salt air accelerates external corrosion at the base of columns, at bolted connections and under insulation, so the survey grid is usually denser in splash and drip zones.

For pressure piping and vessels, readings are taken at condition monitoring locations marked on the inspection drawings, commonly in grids on elbows, tees, dead legs and nozzle necks. Where the owner is working under API 570, API 510 or API 653, the authorized inspector is responsible for remaining-life and interval decisions; Atlantis supplies the thickness data and a report suited to that inspector's records. Storage tank work follows the same pattern, with shell course readings taken on a vertical and circumferential grid.

Shear-wave weld inspection

For welds, the technician uses angle-beam probes, normally 45, 60 or 70 degrees, which send shear waves through the weld and heat-affected zone. A reference level is set from side-drilled holes in a calibration block, the weld is scanned from both sides where the geometry allows, and reflectors above the recording threshold are characterized by position, length and amplitude. Acceptance is taken from the governing code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 12, ASME B31.3, AWS D1.1 for groove welds in structural steel, or API 1104 where an owner specifies ultrasonic examination of pipeline girth welds. Bridge steel is examined to AWS D1.5, which Washington's state transportation work follows. Whether ultrasonic examination can replace radiography on a particular job is decided by the owner, the engineer and the inspector before work starts, and the substitution goes into the written procedure.

Washington regulations that matter

Washington's Department of Labor and Industries runs the state boiler and pressure vessel program. Inspectors who work under it hold a commission after passing the National Board examination and a Washington examination, and the state's rules are collected in Chapter 296-104 of the Washington Administrative Code. Tacoma adds a local requirement: the city requires a license for boiler operators, a requirement the state itself does not impose. Repairs and alterations to pressure equipment follow the National Board Inspection Code. Pipelines are regulated under 49 CFR Parts 192 and 195, and plants subject to OSHA process safety management must keep mechanical-integrity records that show inspection and testing in line with recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice. A thickness report is one of the building blocks of those records.

Who does the work and what the report contains

No Atlantis office exists in Tacoma, so technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope. They are qualified by the company under its written practice, based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, with Level II technicians performing and interpreting the examination and an ASNT Level III approving procedures and reviewing reports. The Level III is the founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. Your own program may require to see the written practice and the technician's qualification file; both can accompany the quote.

Each report identifies the component and drawing, the procedure and revision, instrument, probes and calibration block, couplant, surface condition and temperature, technician and level, and date. Thickness results are given in a grid with nominal and minimum required values alongside, and weld results list each indication by location along the weld, depth, length and amplitude with an accept or reject disposition against the named criteria.

Planning a UT job in Tacoma

The Pacific Northwest climate shapes the schedule more than the temperature does. Tacoma is wet for much of the year, and rain on exposed steel is more of a problem than cold; couplant works in the damp but instruments and cables need protecting, and surface moisture can hide corrosion scale. Summers are mild and dry, which is why many survey campaigns on exterior structures are timed for July through September. Waterfront sites require port-issued credentials and safety orientation, and secure terminal areas limit where a crew can park and carry equipment. Crane work is scheduled around vessel calls, because a crane that is working cannot be climbed, and elevated access needs the owner's fall-protection and lockout procedures. Industrial tideflats sites often require hot-work and confined-space permits, and some call for respirators or other protective equipment, all of which should be settled when the scope is quoted.

Insulated and coated lines need to be opened at test points, and marine coatings may need to be removed locally to give the probe a clean surface. Agreeing who removes and restores them, and who provides lifts or staging, is where most schedule time is saved.

UT, MT or PT for your Tacoma work

Use ultrasonic testing to measure remaining wall and to check welds for flaws below the surface. Use magnetic particle inspection in Tacoma for surface cracks in carbon-steel welds, crane lugs and connection details, and liquid penetrant testing in Tacoma for stainless steel and aluminum. A common sequence on a waterfront structure is a thickness survey to find thinned members, then a surface method on adjacent welds and a shear-wave scan on any repair. For general background, see our ultrasonic testing services overview, and for the state, the inspection services in Washington page.

Training your own technicians

Employers who want their own UT staff can look at UT Level 1 training, UT Level 2 training and the ultrasonic testing simulator. For delivery in the area, see NDT training in Tacoma. A written practice under SNT-TC-1A is the employer's document, and we can draft or review one through written practice development or Level III consulting.

faq.q: Can you examine container crane structures at the Port of Tacoma?
faq.a: Atlantis can perform ultrasonic thickness and weld examination on crane girders, legs and frames when the owner arranges access, permits and a crane outage. We name no terminal as a client; scope, access rules and acceptance criteria come from the owner.

faq.q: Why does salt air matter for ultrasonic thickness surveys in Tacoma?
faq.a: Marine air speeds external corrosion at column bases, bolted joints and beneath coatings or insulation. Surveys therefore use tighter reading grids at splash and drip zones, and coatings often need local removal so the probe contacts clean metal.

faq.q: Do you provide inspectors for API 510, 570 or 653 work?
faq.a: No. The owner's authorized inspector is responsible under those codes. Atlantis performs the ultrasonic examination at the condition monitoring locations and supplies thickness data and a report the inspector can rely on.

faq.q: Can UT replace radiography on a weld in Washington?
faq.a: Sometimes, where the construction code allows and the owner, engineer and authorized inspector agree beforehand. ASME Section VIII, B31.3, AWS D1.1 and API 1104 differ, so the substitution is written into the procedure before scanning begins.

faq.q: What information do you need to quote a Tacoma UT job?
faq.a: Send component lists or drawings, material and nominal thickness, operating temperature, coatings or insulation, access method, governing code and edition, and acceptance criteria. For weld scans, include the joint design and the thickness range.

faq.q: Does rain stop ultrasonic testing?
faq.a: Light rain does not stop couplant-based testing, but wet electronics and slippery access do. Most Tacoma crews schedule exterior work for drier months and use shelters or tents for critical examinations.

faq.q: What does Washington require of the people inspecting boilers and pressure vessels?
faq.a: State inspectors hold a commission earned through the National Board exam and a Washington exam. Separately, Tacoma requires a license for boiler operators. The owner's inspector, not Atlantis, carries those responsibilities.

faq.q: Who qualifies the technicians who travel to my site?
faq.a: The employer qualifies them under its written practice based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician performs and interprets the work and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. Records can be provided with the quote.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in Tacoma, WA
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection and mag particle testing in Tacoma, WA for crane steel, welds, lifting gear and bridge steel. Technicians mobilize to site. Quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Tacoma, Washington
mt.html:
Magnetic particle inspection finds surface and near-surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel, and Atlantis NDT performs it in Tacoma, Washington, on crane structures, welds, lifting gear, bridge steel and heavy fabrications. Technicians are mobilized to your terminal, yard or plant with yokes, particles and calibrated meters and examine to the code you name. Tell us about the work in the Tacoma MT inspection request and we reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle testing is used in Tacoma

Steel is the material of Tacoma's economy. The deepwater port on Commencement Bay handles containers, bulk cargo and heavy lifts, and its cranes, spreaders, chassis and rail equipment put welded joints under repeated load. Spreader bars and twist-lock housings are inspected for cracking as a matter of routine, and the pad eyes, lugs and rigging points that handle lifts are classic magnetic particle targets. The tideflats add fabrication shops, metals processors and repair yards that work on tanks, frames and machinery. State transportation work on steel bridges, as well as railroad and trucking equipment serving the port, rounds out a steady stream of ferromagnetic components with welds that can crack. Magnetic particle testing is portable, immediate and cheap in terms of equipment, which is why it is the first surface method most Tacoma shops reach for on carbon steel.

How the method works and where it stops

The technician magnetizes the part. Any crack, lap or seam that interrupts the magnetic field near the surface leaks flux into the air, and iron particles sprinkled or sprayed on the surface collect there, drawing a visible line over the flaw. Because the method relies on magnetism, it is limited to ferromagnetic materials such as carbon steel, low-alloy steel and martensitic stainless; austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, bronze and most marine alloys cannot be examined this way. It is a surface and near-surface method; a flaw deep within a thick weld will not disturb the field enough to be seen. And direction matters: a crack running parallel to the field produces little leakage, so a second examination at roughly right angles is part of the standard technique. Knowing these limits is how you decide when MT is the right call and when to use another method.

Yokes, particles and lighting in the field

Field work is mostly done with electromagnetic yokes. ASME Section V Article 7 sets the performance check: an AC yoke has to lift at least 10 pounds at the largest pole spacing to be used, and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds. Particles are applied dry or in a liquid carrier, and in visible or fluorescent form. Visible wet particles over a white contrast coat are common on welds and are examined in good white light. Fluorescent particles, viewed under UV-A light in a darkened area, are more sensitive and are used for critical welds and fatigue-prone parts. Rain, spray and wind complicate this outdoors on the waterfront, so an enclosure or tent is often built around the test area, and dry powder is generally avoided when the surface is wet.

The surface must be clean, free of heavy rust, scale, oil and thick coatings, because any of them can hold particles or block them. After the examination, parts are demagnetized when residual fields could affect welding, instruments or later service, and the residual field is checked with a meter.

Governing codes and acceptance

The method is written down in ASME Section V Article 7, with ASTM E1444 and ASTM E709 as supporting standards. Acceptance depends on the code that built or repairs the item. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 applies to pressure vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 and Table 341.3.2 to process piping, AWS D1.1 to structural steel and AWS D1.5 to bridges. Steel crane structures are usually governed by AWS D1.1 or the manufacturer's specification, and a lifting-device owner's program may add its own criteria. Where the work supports API 510, 570 or 653 inspection, the owner's authorized inspector remains responsible; Atlantis carries out the examination and returns the data. Each job has a written procedure approved by an ASNT Level III, covering surface preparation, magnetizing method, particles, field check and acceptance criteria.

Washington's regulatory setting

The state's boiler and pressure vessel program, run by the Department of Labor and Industries, commissions inspectors through the National Board examination plus a Washington examination, and its rules sit in Chapter 296-104 of the Washington Administrative Code. The City of Tacoma separately requires a license for boiler operators. Repairs and alterations follow the National Board Inspection Code, and plants subject to OSHA process safety management document inspection and testing against recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice. For a Tacoma job these rules rarely change the technique, but they decide who has to witness a repair and which records the owner must keep.

Personnel and reporting

Tacoma has no Atlantis office; crews travel to your site for the agreed scope. Technicians are qualified under the company's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, with a Level II examining and interpreting and an ASNT Level III approving procedures and reviewing reports. The founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, holds that Level III role. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001.

The report records component and weld IDs, material and surface condition, the procedure and revision, yoke or equipment ID and its check results, particle type and carrier, white-light or UV-A readings, the technician and level, and each indication with location, orientation and length. Indications are dispositioned as accept or reject against the stated criteria, normally with a photograph and a sketch so repair crews know where to grind.

Planning an MT job in Tacoma

Moisture is the dominant planning issue. Tacoma's wet months bring rain, mist and condensation to exposed steel, and wet particles need a clean, reasonably dry surface to work reliably. Winter days are short and gray, which suits fluorescent work in a tent but demands working lights for visible-particle jobs. Temperatures usually remain well within the range particle materials tolerate. Waterfront access is controlled, so credentials, safety orientation and escort rules should be arranged early. Hydrocarbon and chemical facilities restrict ignition sources, which affects electrical yokes and extension cords, and prods are typically barred. Elevated crane structures need the owner's lockout and fall-protection procedures, and the work is timed around vessel calls so the crane is free.

Salt deposits and marine coatings need attention too. Chloride deposits are removed before examination and the surface cleaned again after, particularly where the steel will be repainted or welded.

MT, PT or UT: choosing the method

Pick magnetic particle inspection when surface cracks in carbon steel are the concern and speed matters. If the material is stainless steel or aluminum, liquid penetrant testing in Tacoma is the surface method to use, and for wall loss or hidden weld flaws, ultrasonic testing in Tacoma is. Our national magnetic particle testing page covers the method generally, the Washington inspection hub lists related services, and the guide to MT versus PT compares the two surface methods.

Training your own MT examiners

Employers who want in-house examiners can start with MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training, and the magnetic particle testing complete guide is a good primer. For delivery details, see NDT training in Tacoma.

Crane and lifting-gear examinations in practice

Port equipment shows the pattern of fatigue clearly. Cracks start at weld toes where a stiffener meets a girder flange, at the corners of access openings, at the roots of cope cuts and around attachment welds for walkways and cable supports. A technician climbing a crane to examine these areas needs a short, clear list of locations from the owner's engineer or the manufacturer's inspection manual, plus a plan for lighting and the particle system. Spreaders and lifting beams are generally examined on the ground at a maintenance bay, where fluorescent particles and a darkened booth are easier to arrange. Findings are returned with sketches that reference the crane's own member designations so that the repair plan can be written quickly.

Examinations of this kind are usually scheduled as part of a planned outage. Giving us the outage window and the crane identification at the quote stage lets the procedure and equipment be prepared in advance.

Repair verification

After a crack is found, MT is used again to check that the excavation is clear before welding and to examine the completed repair. Both examinations belong in the record, because they show the defect was removed rather than welded over. Where the repair is on a pressure-retaining item, the National Board Inspection Code and the owner's repair procedure dictate who witnesses the examination, so mention any repair organization or inspector in the request.

faq.q: Can magnetic particle inspection be done outdoors in Tacoma's wet weather?
faq.a: Yes with protection. Wet particles need a reasonably dry, clean surface, so technicians use tents or shelters, and fluorescent work gets a darkened enclosure. Heavy rain or standing water on the surface will stop the examination until conditions improve.

faq.q: Does MT work on stainless steel and aluminum parts at the port?
faq.a: Not on austenitic stainless steel, aluminum or bronze, because they are not ferromagnetic. Liquid penetrant testing is the surface method for those materials, and ultrasonic testing is used where the concern is below the surface.

faq.q: What is the yoke lifting-power check?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 7 requires an AC yoke to lift at least 10 pounds at the maximum pole spacing, and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds. The technician proves this with a test weight before examining.

faq.q: Can you inspect crane spreaders and lifting lugs?
faq.a: Yes. Lifting lugs, pad eyes, spreader components and attachment welds are common MT targets. The owner provides access, the manufacturer's or engineer's inspection criteria and an outage window, and Atlantis delivers a report with sketches.

faq.q: Are prods allowed on pressure equipment?
faq.a: Many owners prohibit them, since arcing can burn the metal and spark in hydrocarbon areas. Yokes avoid that risk. The technique used is the one your specification permits, and restrictions are flagged during quoting.

faq.q: Who decides whether an indication is acceptable?
faq.a: The acceptance criteria in your code or specification decide, applied by the technician and reviewed by an ASNT Level III. On API-inspected equipment the owner's authorized inspector makes repair and fitness decisions from our data.

faq.q: Does marine coating interfere with magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: Thick coatings reduce sensitivity and heavy salt or rust hold particles, so surfaces are cleaned and thin coatings are assessed against what the procedure allows. Where coating is too heavy, it is removed locally.

faq.q: What should I include in a Tacoma MT quote request?
faq.a: List the components or weld numbers, material and surface condition, governing code and edition, acceptance criteria, access method, and any site rules on electrical equipment or permits. Drawings or photographs of the areas of concern speed up the quote.

pt.title: Liquid Penetrant Testing & Dye Penetrant | Tacoma, WA
pt.description: Dye penetrant inspection and liquid penetrant testing in Tacoma, WA for stainless, aluminum, marine alloys and welds. Technicians mobilize to your site. Quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Tacoma, Washington
pt.html:
Dye penetrant inspection reveals surface-breaking cracks on any clean, non-porous metal, and Atlantis NDT performs liquid penetrant testing in Tacoma, Washington, on stainless piping, aluminum, marine alloys and welds in carbon steel. Technicians are mobilized to your yard, plant or vessel-side location with a written procedure and the right penetrant system. Describe the parts in the Tacoma PT inspection request and we reply within one business day.

Where penetrant testing is used in Tacoma

A harbor city has more non-magnetic metal than most. Marine hardware in stainless steel, bronze and aluminum, propeller and shaft components, heat exchangers in cooling water systems, and aluminum workboat and barge structures are all part of the waterfront economy around Commencement Bay. Pulp and paperboard mills run stainless steel digesters, liquor piping and heat exchangers where corrosion cracking is a recognized damage mechanism. Food processors, water treatment works and chemical storage sites on the tideflats use stainless tanks and piping. Welds on carbon steel crane parts and tank nozzles can also be examined by penetrant when the weld shape makes a yoke difficult to place. In each case the question is the same: is there a crack open to the surface that a visual check would miss?

What penetrant testing detects and what it misses

Penetrant is a low-viscosity liquid that is drawn into surface cracks by capillary action. After the excess is removed, a developer draws the trapped liquid out so it appears as a bright mark on the surface. Since the liquid has to get in, the method detects only flaws that are open to the surface; a crack closed by peening, grinding, corrosion product or paint will not show. It cannot detect subsurface flaws, internal corrosion or lack of fusion inside a weld. It works on porous materials only with difficulty. Its great advantage is that it is nearly independent of material: ferrous, nonferrous, magnetic or not, metal or ceramic, a clean non-porous surface will show its cracks. It also shows the full length of a crack at a glance, which makes it popular for fatigue checks.

Penetrant systems and how the test is run

A system has three parts: cleaner, penetrant and developer, and they must be used as a matched set. Penetrants are visible dye, viewed in white light, or fluorescent, viewed under UV-A light in a darkened area for greater sensitivity. Removal can be by water wash, solvent wipe or an emulsifier step. Solvent-removable visible penetrant is the field workhorse because it needs no water supply and travels easily to a crane boom or a tank. The sequence is cleaning, application, dwell, removal of surface excess, developer, and examination within the procedure's time window.

Temperature limits matter in the Pacific Northwest more than people expect. ASME Section V Article 6 treats 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit as the standard range for the part and the materials. Tacoma's cool, wet winters can put steel surfaces below 40 degrees at dawn or at the water's edge, and then either the surface is warmed and dried or a procedure qualified for the lower temperature is used. Penetrant also does not tolerate wet surfaces; moisture in a crack keeps the penetrant out, so rain-soaked steel must be dried before the test.

Codes and acceptance criteria

Penetrant examination is carried out to the construction code. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 covers vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 and Table 341.3.2 cover process piping, AWS D1.1 covers structural welds, and the method itself sits in ASME Section V Article 6 with ASTM E165 as a general industry practice. For stainless and nickel alloys, penetrant materials with controlled halogen and sulfur are used, since residues can attack those alloys, and the lot certificates are kept with the job. Where results support an API 510, 570 or 653 inspection, the owner's authorized inspector remains responsible for the inspection and Atlantis delivers the data. A procedure approved by an ASNT Level III governs each job.

Washington and Tacoma rules

Pressure equipment in Washington falls under the state's boiler and pressure vessel program, administered by the Department of Labor and Industries, with commissioned inspectors who have passed the National Board and Washington examinations; the rules are in Chapter 296-104 of the Washington Administrative Code. Tacoma also requires a license for boiler operators. Repairs and alterations follow the National Board Inspection Code. Environmental rules matter too: waterfront and tideflats sites are subject to stormwater and waste controls, so penetrant cleaners, wipes and developer residues are handled and disposed of under the site's own waste procedures, and shoreline work needs spill precautions. Ask the owner which products are approved on site before the materials are ordered.

Personnel and reports

The company keeps no office in Tacoma; technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope. They are qualified under Atlantis's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, with Level II performing and interpreting the test and an ASNT Level III approving procedures and reviewing reports. That Level III is the founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 certification are held by Atlantis.

The report lists the part or weld ID, material, surface condition, the penetrant system and batch numbers, dwell time, surface temperature at application, developer, lighting measurements, the technician and level, and every indication with location and size. Each indication carries an accept or reject disposition against the stated criteria, with a photograph where it helps.

Planning a PT job in Tacoma

Dry steel and a clean surface are the two things that decide whether a penetrant job runs smoothly. Rain and mist are frequent, so work on exposed steel is scheduled for dry windows or carried out under a shelter, and salt deposits, mill scale and marine paint are removed before cleaning. Cold mornings may need the surface warmed. Fluorescent examination needs a dark enclosure, which on the waterfront means a tent anchored against wind. Safety orientation and port credentials are required at secure terminals, and chemical use near water has to be agreed with the site's environmental staff. Where parts are in service, operating schedules and lockout arrangements should be set when the scope is quoted.

Penetrant on marine and corrosion-resistant alloys

Marine duty is hard on metal. Stainless steel in chloride environments can develop pitting and stress corrosion cracks that are tight and shallow, and aluminum in salt air suffers crevice corrosion and fatigue at welds. A properly cleaned surface and adequate dwell give penetrant the chance to enter those fine cracks. For critical parts, fluorescent penetrant with a sensitive developer is usually specified. After testing, residues are removed, since leftover penetrant can attract contaminants and developer can interfere with later coatings or welding.

PT, MT or UT for Tacoma work

Choose penetrant testing for surface cracks in non-magnetic metals, and where a part's geometry makes magnetizing impractical. For carbon steel where speed counts, magnetic particle inspection in Tacoma is often faster, and for wall loss or buried weld flaws, ultrasonic testing in Tacoma is the right tool. Our national penetrant testing page and the Washington inspection hub give more context, and the guide to ASME Article 6 explains the method requirements.

Training your own penetrant examiners

Employers that want their own penetrant technicians can start with PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training, with a browser-based penetrant testing simulator for practice. Delivery details are on the Tacoma training page.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing find cracks in marine stainless steel at Tacoma's waterfront?
faq.a: Yes, if the crack is open to the surface and the metal is clean and dry. Fluorescent penetrant is often chosen for fine corrosion cracks. Cracks filled with salt, scale or paint must be cleaned out first or they will not show.

faq.q: Does cold, wet weather prevent liquid penetrant testing?
faq.a: It can. ASME Section V Article 6 treats 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit as the standard range, and wet surfaces keep penetrant out of cracks. Work is delayed, the surface warmed and dried, or a procedure qualified for lower temperatures is used.

faq.q: What is the difference between visible and fluorescent penetrant?
faq.a: Visible penetrant is a colored dye seen in white light, while fluorescent penetrant glows under UV-A light in a darkened area and detects finer cracks. The procedure states which system is used and which lighting checks apply.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing detect subsurface flaws or wall loss?
faq.a: No. It only shows discontinuities open to the surface. Wall loss and internal weld flaws require ultrasonic testing, and a surface crack that has been closed by grinding or filled with debris will not show until it is cleaned.

faq.q: How are penetrant chemicals and waste handled near the water?
faq.a: Under the site's own environmental and waste procedures. Cleaners and wipes are collected and disposed of as the owner requires, and the products used are agreed in advance. Tideflats sites often have stormwater rules that restrict what can be released.

faq.q: Is penetrant testing suitable for aluminum workboat structures?
faq.a: Yes. Aluminum is non-magnetic, so penetrant is the usual surface method for weld cracks and fatigue cracks. The surface must be clean, and the procedure is qualified for the alloy and temperature.

faq.q: Who evaluates the indications?
faq.a: A Level II technician evaluates them against the acceptance criteria in your code, and an ASNT Level III reviews the report. For API-inspected equipment, the owner's authorized inspector decides on repair and service from the data we provide.

faq.q: What should I send to get a penetrant quote?
faq.a: Send the part or weld list, material and finish, governing code and edition, acceptance criteria, access, and site rules on chemicals and waste. Photographs of the surfaces help us judge the cleaning needed before the crew mobilizes.
